Using power responsibly

Leaving room is still a choice.

Holding back can give someone room. It can also leave someone exposed.

A closer lookOpen the shared interactive reader ↗

The interactive example has its own motion control. Scroll inside it if you need more room.

A philosophical and theological argument

The argument asks how power can help other people make real choices. Taking over every decision can remove the freedom we say we want to support.

But holding back is not always helpful. If someone is taking away another person’s freedom, protection may be needed. Ask who gains room to act, and who is left carrying the cost.

Words used here
agency
A person’s ability to make choices and have a meaningful effect on what happens.
kenosis
A Christian term often translated as “self-emptying.” Here it means using power while making room for others to act.
Read the fuller explanation

The kenotic argument treats power as something governed by love rather than exhausted by control. Making room for another agent is a positive commitment: their choices must be consequential enough to count as their own.

That commitment is not an absolute rule against intervention. The same argument retains boundaries and responsibility for protection. If one agent is consuming another’s effective freedom, leaving the arrangement alone can preserve domination rather than make room for agency.

This is a philosophical boundary to examine, not an instruction about your own situation. Ask whose room is growing, whose is shrinking, and what evidence would challenge the comfortable description of your choice.

Where this comes from: Power, restraint and responsibility

Theological and philosophical argument

A philosophical and theological argument

Distinguishes the ability to use power from permission and responsibility. It makes room for both restraint and protection. It is not a scientific law.

Read the full source note

Kenotic governance and shared responsibility

Capability, moral permission and an obligation to exercise power are distinguished. Restraint must also be examined where one agent destroys another’s effective agency. The argument remains defeasible and is not a physical derivation.
